title: India Has Never Qualified. In Kerala, the World Cup Fever Is Louder Than Anywhere.
excerpt: Giant banners of Messi and Neymar stretch across Malappuram's streets. Fan clubs pool lakhs. And Keralite diaspora communities from Dubai to Dallas are organising screening events. The 2026 World Cup starts tomorrow.
body:
The World Cup begins tomorrow. In Kerala, it has already started.

Across the state's narrow roads and crowded town squares, a transformation is underway that happens once every four years, as predictable as the monsoon and nearly as dramatic. Giant banners — some stretching across entire streets — are going up in Malappuram, Palakkad, Kochi, Thrissur, and Kozhikode. They feature the faces of Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, Neymar, and Kylian Mbappé, rendered in vivid colour and mounted on makeshift bamboo frames. Yellow flares mark the territory of Brazil supporters. Blue and white streamers announce Argentina's faithful.

India has never qualified for the FIFA World Cup. This has not dampened enthusiasm in the slightest.

Kerala's relationship with football is unlike any other Indian state's. While the rest of the country has historically been consumed by cricket, Kerala adopted the global game decades ago — a legacy of its port cities, its Gulf diaspora connections, its high literacy rates and exposure to European television, and a Communist sporting culture that favoured the collective over the individual. When Brazil and Argentina meet on the pitch, Malappuram takes sides. When Portugal scores, Kozhikode celebrates. Neighbourhoods divide into rival fan clubs with names, flags, social media accounts, and annual budgets.

## The Biggest World Cup in History

The 2026 edition, kicking off on June 11 in Mexico City with hosts Mexico against Bosnia and Herzegovina, is the largest World Cup ever staged. For the first time, 48 nations will compete across 104 matches in 16 cities spanning the United States, Canada, and Mexico. The tournament runs through July 19.

For Indian fans — and Kerala's millions in particular — there were anxious weeks when it appeared the tournament would not even be broadcast in the country. Negotiations between FIFA and JioStar reportedly stalled over valuation disagreements, leaving India, one of the world's largest growing football markets, without a confirmed broadcaster. The deadlock was broken only on June 1, when Zee Entertainment secured the rights for approximately $60 million, roughly 40 per cent less than FIFA's initial asking price.

Matches will air on the newly launched Unite8 Sports network (Hindi and English feeds) on television, with live streaming on the Zee5 app. The deal covers 39 FIFA events through 2034, including the 2030 World Cup and the 2027 Women's World Cup. Zee has said it has scaled its streaming infrastructure to support millions of concurrent viewers.

## From Malappuram to Dallas, the Fan Clubs Mobilise

What makes Kerala's World Cup culture unique is its grassroots organisation. In Malappuram, widely regarded as the football capital of India, neighbourhoods form official fan clubs months before the tournament. Rival groups for Brazil, Argentina, Portugal, Germany, France, and the Netherlands put up banners, organise screening events, commission murals, and sometimes hire DJs for match nights. The spending is not trivial — some fan groups reportedly pool lakhs of rupees for their efforts.

This culture travels with the diaspora. Keralites in the Gulf states — the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait, and Bahrain — have carried the tradition with them, organising World Cup screenings and fan gatherings in cities where large Malayali populations live and work. In the United States, Malayali associations in cities like Houston, Dallas, Chicago, and New Jersey have announced screening events for the 2026 edition, many timed around the India-heavy scheduling slots.

For NRIs across North America, this World Cup is uniquely accessible. Matches will be played in 16 host cities including New York, Los Angeles, Miami, Houston, Dallas, Seattle, San Francisco, and Toronto. For the first time, attending a World Cup match does not require an international flight. Ticket prices start at $35 for group-stage matches, and FIFA's resale platform has made secondary-market purchases safer, though premium knockout-round seats remain steep.

## No Country, But an Identity

India's absence from the tournament has never diluted Kerala's passion — if anything, it has freed fans to adopt teams without the complications of nationalism. A supporter from Thrissur who has watched every World Cup since 1998 can be a lifelong Argentina loyalist without contradiction. A teenager in Palakkad can paint his face in the colours of the Dutch tricolour without irony.

This year's groups have added intrigue. Brazil, perennial favourites and Kerala's most popular side, face Morocco, Scotland, and Haiti in Group C. Argentina, the defending champions with an ageing Messi making what is widely expected to be his final World Cup, are in Group H alongside Colombia, Senegal, and Uzbekistan. Portugal, with Ronaldo at 41 embarking on a record sixth World Cup campaign, sit in Group K.

The tournament's expansion to 48 teams also means debut appearances for nations like Cabo Verde, Curaçao, Jordan, and Uzbekistan — and more matches spread across time zones that will test even the most dedicated fans in India's IST.

## A State That Watches Together

As the first match approaches — Mexico vs Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Estadio Azteca — the banners in Kerala will be at full mast. Television sets in tea shops, barbershops, and toddy parlours will be tuned in. Group chats among Malayali communities worldwide will be buzzing. And in a state that has never produced a World Cup footballer, the world's biggest sporting event will be lived as intensely as anywhere on earth.

The monsoon arrives in Kerala this week too. It will not keep anyone indoors. That is what the football is for.
